title: Copenhagen team maps full Taxol (paclitaxel) pathway and makes the cancer drug in tobacco plants

Don't expect tobacco-grown chemo soon. The genes must first become a permanent part of the plant.
The hope: a cheaper drug for poorer countries, grown in a cousin of the plant behind cigarettes.

caption:
A cousin of the plant behind cigarettes may one day help make chemotherapy cheaper.

Taxol, also called paclitaxel, treats breast, ovarian and lung cancer. It was first found in the bark of the Pacific yew, and stripping bark kills slow-growing trees. Today it is made by extracting related compounds from yew plants and turning them into the drug through a long chain of chemical reactions.

For decades, scientists knew where the tree started and where it ended up, but not every step in between. On November 23, a team at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark published the complete pathway in Nature Chemical Biology. They put more than 20 yew genes into Nicotiana benthamiana, a fast-growing tobacco species used in labs, and its leaves made Taxol at levels comparable to yew bark.

"We now have a blueprint, essentially a recipe," said senior author Sotirios Kampranis. It could also work in yeast.

The catch: the genes had to be added to each new batch of plants. Greenhouse production needs plants that carry them permanently, and any new source would still need regulators' approval. Nothing changes for patients today.

The team's goal is a cheaper drug for countries that struggle to afford it.

Source: University of Copenhagen, Nature Chemical Biology, Medical Daily
